newsitem.title: USA: Coffee rises again as growers to cut exports.
newsitem.headline: Coffee rises again as growers to cut exports.

text.p: Coffee prices extended their dizzy rally Thursday fed by supply worries that sent the market to its highest levels in 16 months.
Corn and wheat prices closed lower as the outlook for exports weakened. Crude oil and heating oil fell on the belief that supplies are adequate for the winter.

On New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, March delivery coffee ended 4.75 cents at 140.05 cents a pound after surging to a new life-of-contract high of 142.00 cents, the highest price for coffee on weekly charts since September 1995.
"There is just not a lot of coffee out there," said PaineWebber analyst Bernard Savaiko.

A long dockworkers' strike in Colombia, prospects for a smaller Brazilian crop this year and news the Association of Coffee Producing Countries agreed to cut exports have kept worries about coffee supplies on the boil, Savaiko said.
Prices rose for an eighth straight day on talk that the coffee producers association, meeting in Rio De Janeiro, had already agreed to a cut in coffee exports in the first half of this year.

After the market closed, the association announced it agreed to cut member coffee exports by 1.3 million bags between January and June 1997, including 300,000 bags of Arabica "mild" beans highly sought by American and European roasters.
The producers association includes the top two exporters, Brazil and Colombia, along with other major producers like Indonesia and Kenya.

Bullish sentiments ran so strong that traders shrugged off news during the day of a deal to end the nine-day dockworkers strike at Colombia's port of Buenaventura. The labor action had blocked shipments of more than 300,000 bags of coffee.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn and wheat prices closed lower as the outlook for exports weakened due to strong overseas competition.
March corn closed 1/4 cent a bushel lower at $2.70-1/4 and March wheat 3-1/2 cents a bushel lower at $3.75-3/4.

European and Australian officials this week raised their forecasts for wheat production, pressuring world prices. Traders also said India, which had been rumored to need up to 750,000 metric tons of wheat, would likely buy far less.
"They don't think India will buy much more than the 50,000 tons because there have been good rains recently in India," said analyst Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter Reynolds.

News that China was back in the world market as a corn exporter kept a lid on corn prices. A U.S. government grain official said Thursday that China sold at least 300,000 metric tons of corn in recent weeks.
March soybeans bucked the lower trend in grains, closing up 3/4 cent a bushel at $7.41-1/4 as commercial grain firms entered the market to buy futures, traders said.
New York precious metals ended higher led by a strong rally in silver, but not before gold saw new 40-month lows.
March silver at the New York Mercantile Exchange's COMEX division ended up 15.2 cents at $4.875 an ounce.

"There's been a dramatic outperformance by silver over gold in recent weeks, leading to talk of some large spread plays between the two metals, but the market remains very short and sentiment is still bearish overall," fund manager Jeff Kowal of Friedberg Mercantile Group in Toronto said.
February gold closed up 80 cents at $352.50 an ounce after setting a new life-of-contract low of $347.30.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices ended mostly lower amid selling in heating oil fueled by ideas that supplies are ample for winter and the weather will stay relatively moderate.

February heating oil closed 0.54 cent a gallon lower at 66.35 cents, with February crude oil ending down 6 cents a barrel at $24.18. February gasoline rose 0.20 cent a gallon at 68.42 cents, the only contract to gain in the oil complex.
